entities.name: Jean I Le Meingre
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Jean I Le Meingre, known by his distinguished epithet Boucicaut, was a prominent French noble and Marshal of France whose military career significantly shaped the early and middle phases of the Hundred Years' War. Born into a distinguished family in Touraine, his life spanned the tumultuous mid-14th century (died 1367-03-23), an era defined by Anglo-French conflict and the devastating impact of the Black Death. His strategic acumen and martial prowess were instrumental in defending French interests against English incursions, establishing him as a key figure in the Capetian and early Valois military aristocracy.

Boucicaut's military service began early, participating in campaigns that aimed to consolidate French royal authority and repel English advances. He distinguished himself in various skirmishes and sieges, including the defense of the French frontier in Picardy and Normandy. His rise through the ranks culminated in his appointment as Marshal of France in 1356, a testament to his tactical skill and loyalty, especially following the catastrophic French defeat at the Battle of Poitiers. In this capacity, he played a crucial role in the chevauchées and counter-offensives that characterized the conflict, often employing guerrilla tactics and scorched-earth strategies to disrupt English supply lines and morale.

His contributions were vital in maintaining a degree of French resistance during periods of severe royal weakness and internal strife, particularly under King John II and the regency of the future Charles V. Boucicaut's efforts helped to preserve key French territories and fortresses, laying groundwork for the later reconquests under Charles V. His legacy was further cemented by his son, Jean II Le Meingre, also known as Boucicaut, who inherited his father's martial reputation and achieved even greater renown as a Marshal of France and a crusader.
